client: Hey Luna, I've been really anxious lately about meeting my partner's friends this weekend. I'm worried they won't accept me, and it's been weighing heavily on my mind. I'm not sure if talking about it will help, but I thought I'd give it a shot.
therapist: Hi there! It sounds like you're carrying a lot of anxiety about meeting your partner's friends, and that's completely understandable. It's natural to worry about how others will perceive you. What are some of the specific thoughts that come up when you think about this meeting?

client: Well, I keep thinking that I won't fit in, that I'll say something stupid or awkward. I also worry that they might not like me, and that will make things really uncomfortable between me and my partner. It's just a lot of pressure, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're really concerned about fitting in and making a good impression, and that's adding a lot of pressure. It's normal to worry about these things, but it can be helpful to look at the evidence. What are some of the reasons you think they might accept and like you?

client: I guess my partner has told me that his friends are really welcoming and open-minded. They've also heard a lot about me, and they seem excited to finally meet me. But I still can't shake the feeling that I might mess up or that they won't like me. It's hard to trust that everything will go well.
therapist: It's great to hear that your partner has shared positive things about his friends and that they're looking forward to meeting you. It's completely normal to still have some doubts and worries, especially when it comes to meeting new people. What do you think might help you feel more confident or prepared for the meeting?

client: I think if I could practice some small talk or think of a few topics to bring up, it might help me feel more prepared. But it's hard because I get so caught up in my own head, and I worry that I'll overthink everything and still end up feeling awkward.
therapist: It sounds like having some conversation starters ready could help you feel more prepared and less anxious. It's totally normal to overthink things, but preparing a few topics might give you a sense of control. What are some topics or questions you think would be good to bring up during the meeting?

client: I could talk about my hobbies or ask them about theirs. Maybe ask about their jobs or any upcoming plans they have. But I'm still worried that I'll freeze up and forget everything I planned to say. It's a bit overwhelming, you know?
therapist: It's a good idea to have some topics like your hobbies and their interests ready. It can definitely help to ease into the conversation. It's also totally normal to feel a bit overwhelmed and worried about freezing up. What do you think might help you stay present and engaged during the conversation, even if you feel a bit nervous?

client: I think deep breathing might help me stay calm and present. Maybe taking a few deep breaths before I speak could ease my nerves a bit. But I'm still skeptical about how much it will actually help in the moment.
therapist: Deep breathing is a great strategy to help manage anxiety and stay present. It can be really effective, even if it feels a bit skeptical at first. Have you tried deep breathing before, and if so, did you notice any difference in how you felt?

client: I have tried deep breathing a few times, and sometimes it helps a little, but other times I still feel really anxious. I guess I just worry that it won't be enough to overcome how nervous I am about this meeting. It's hard to trust that it will make a big difference.
therapist: It's totally understandable to have mixed feelings about deep breathing and whether it will be enough to help with your anxiety. It's a common concern, and it's okay to feel skeptical. What do you think might help you feel more confident in using deep breathing, or are there other strategies you might consider to support you during the meeting?

client: I think it would help if I had a few more tools in my toolbox, not just deep breathing. Maybe some positive affirmations or a quick mental checklist to remind myself of my strengths. But it's still hard to imagine myself feeling completely at ease, especially when I'm so worried about making a good impression.
therapist: It sounds like adding a few more strategies to your toolbox could help you feel more prepared and confident. Positive affirmations and a mental checklist of your strengths are great ideas. They can remind you of your value and help shift your focus away from your worries. What are some affirmations or strengths you might want to focus on before the meeting?

client: I could focus on affirmations like "I am worthy of acceptance" and "I am capable of making meaningful connections." My strengths include being a good listener and having a good sense of humor. But it's still a bit daunting to think about putting all this into practice, especially when I'm so worried about how it will go.
therapist: It's great that you've identified some powerful affirmations and strengths to focus on. These can be really helpful in boosting your confidence. It's completely normal to still feel a bit daunting, especially when you're worried about the outcome. What do you think might help you feel more at ease as you prepare for the meeting, even with these lingering concerns?

client: I think it might help if I could talk to my partner more about my worries and get some reassurance from them. Knowing that they understand and support me could make a big difference. But I also don't want to burden them with my anxiety, so I'm a bit torn about that.
therapist: It's really important to communicate your feelings with your partner, especially when you're feeling anxious. Their support can be a huge comfort, and they might be able to offer you some reassurance that helps ease your worries. At the same time, it's natural to worry about burdening them. What do you think might be a good way to approach the conversation with your partner so that you can share your feelings without feeling like you're putting too much on them?
